all.title: Interactive System Development Life Cycle Stages

concepts.name: extended reality
concepts.definition: Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

defining_facts.text: Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

The X in Extended Reality (XR) can be read as a variable, not only as part of 'extended', and its values such as A, V, and M denote augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR), while its many possible values form present or future immersive technologies.

Although adoption statistics can be misleading, earlier use forecasts discussed in the course indicate that extended reality, which covers augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR), has commercial potential in video games (about 34% or more than one third of applications), healthcare, engineering, live events, video entertainment, real estate, retail, and military (about 4% of application areas, a figure that may change); because worldwide military budgets are huge, even 4% is a large monetary amount, so penetration in the commercial space can be expected both percentage-wise and value-wise.

concepts.name: virtual reality
concepts.definition: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.

defining_facts.text: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
Augmented reality (AR) alters the ongoing perception of the real world, whereas virtual reality (VR) completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment.

A virtual reality (VR) system does not require the physical existence of an object or place, because it creates a virtual environment, whereas an augmented reality (AR) or mixed reality (MR) system requires the place being experienced to exist.

The early era in the historical evolution of virtual reality (VR) is the period before modern digital computers were developed in the 1940s, and although not everything was present in that era, a few key developments were conceptually similar to immersive virtual reality experiences.

In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.

The flight simulator concept introduced for the first time in 1928 by Edwin A. Link evolved into sophisticated flight simulators with multiple sensors that provide an immersive experience, and this early development is considered a precursor to modern multi-sensory immersive virtual reality (VR).

The main objective of any virtual reality (VR) system is to let the user experience an artificial environment through sensory stimuli provided by the computer, not only for sight and sound but for all sensory organs.

There are broadly two major issues in experiencing virtual reality (VR): the technological issue of how to generate suitable sensory stimuli for the artificial environment, and the psychological issue of how to perceive those stimuli suitably, a human-factor issue that technology does not address and that is likely to differ between users.

The technological and psychological issues in virtual reality (VR) give rise to two major concerns that appear in almost every literature on VR technology or experience, namely immersion and presence.
The causes of cyber sickness are broadly internal factors and external factors, and external factors comprise hardware and virtual reality (VR) content.

Cyber sickness can be independent of age when users view general virtual reality (VR) content, while age may be a factor for controllable content, making the age relationship clearer for controllable content.

A possible reason for increased cyber sickness among female head-mounted display (HMD) users is inter-pupillary distance (IPD) fit, because IPD determines stereoscopic vision and a greater proportion of females may have trouble finding a good fit; this implies virtual reality (VR) displays should have a wider IPD adjustable range for female users.

Virtual reality (VR) recreates realistic movement and visual environments, making the user feel as if in a real-world environment; therefore, users with motion sickness (MS) susceptibility tend also to have cyber sickness susceptibility.

Prior exposure to virtual reality (VR) systems and repeated exposure to VR can reduce the effect of motion sickness (MS) susceptibility on cyber sickness and reduce cyber sickness severity over time, so the positive correlation may not hold if either or both conditions are satisfied.

A user's physical position affects cyber sickness susceptibility: using a virtual reality (VR) system in a standing posture is likely to induce more cyber sickness, or more severe cyber sickness, than using the same system while sitting.

A virtual reality (VR) system is designed to create interactions that make the user feel immersed, and the amount of presence and the quality of the overall experience depend on fooling the user's perceptual system into believing the virtual system is the familiar real world.
Virtual reality generally provides the brain with sensory signals that are inconsistent with the user's real-life experiences and behavior.

One possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body adapts to the new stimuli, making the user unaware of any flaws in the system and causing the user to believe that the virtual system is the real world rather than an artificial system.

Another possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body may not be able to adapt, causing increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness, that is, dizziness, nausea, or a large set of different symptoms experienced while using virtual reality systems.
An understanding of human perception is needed to design a better virtual reality (VR) system or to identify and resolve flaws in a given system.

In the Unity editor interface, the preference tab lets the developer select extended reality (XR) settings for three system types: virtual reality, which simulates a completely artificial environment around the user; mixed reality, which combines Unity's own environment with the user's real world environment and allows the environments to interact; and augmented reality, which provides layers of content over a digital view of the real world.

concepts.name: head-mounted display
concepts.definition: The formative years of virtual reality are the second phase of its historical evolution, roughly 1950 to 1990 after computers appeared in the 1940s, beginning with development of head-mounted displays (HMDs) in the 1950s and ending with popularization of the term virtual reality in the late 1980s.

defining_facts.text: The formative years of virtual reality are the second phase of its historical evolution, roughly 1950 to 1990 after computers appeared in the 1940s, beginning with development of head-mounted displays (HMDs) in the 1950s and ending with popularization of the term virtual reality in the late 1980s.

In the 1950s, especially toward the latter half of the decade, people started working on and considering different types of head-mounted displays (HMDs), a new kind of computer display that was less common than regular computer monitors.
In 1961, engineers at Philco Corporation developed an early head-mounted display (HMD) that could track users' motion but was bulky and uncomfortable to wear.
In 1965, Tom Furness and colleagues at the Wright-Patterson Air Force Base worked on visually coupled systems for pilots that consisted of head-mounted displays (HMDs).
In 1967, Sutherland developed the Sword of Damocles, a head-mounted display (HMD), and was the first to demonstrate an HMD with head tracking and computer-generated imagery.

In 1985, Scott Fisher and colleagues at the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) developed and launched Virtual Visual Environment Display (VIVED), the first commercially viable and commercially available stereoscopic head-tracked head-mounted display (HMD) with a wide field of view.

The three broad types of visual displays are head-mounted displays (HMDs), which are wearable and mobile, world-fixed displays, which are not wearable and are stationary, and regular displays, which are mobile or can be stationary.
Although head-mounted displays (HMDs) can be used as input to track head motion, their primary use is as a display device.
A head-mounted display (HMD) is a sophisticated piece of equipment that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components within its package.

A head-mounted display (HMD) places images directly in front of the user's eyes using one or two small screens, with one screen providing monoscopic viewing and two screens providing stereoscopic viewing, and stereoscopic HMDs are more common than monoscopic HMDs.
Head-mounted displays (HMDs) can be further categorized into three types: non-see-through, optical see-through, and video see-through.

Non-see-through HMDs are typically used in virtual reality (VR), optical see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented reality (AR), and video see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented virtuality, in which real-world images or videos appear in real time within an artificial or virtual environment.

concepts.name: usability
concepts.definition: Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user.

defining_facts.text: Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user.

The International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 standard defines usability as the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

The three crucial aspects of the International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 usability definition are that a usable product is intended for a specified group of users rather than everybody, that it supports a specified set of goals rather than every conceivable feature, and that it is designed for a specified context of use rather than all usage scenarios.

The three measures of usability are effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction; effectiveness is whether the user can do what they want to do, efficiency is how fast the user can do what they want to do, and satisfaction is how satisfied the user is when using the system.

concepts.name: software development kit
concepts.definition: In practical virtual reality (VR) development, a developer may use a software development kit (SDK) for a particular headset or platform to handle lowest-level, platform-specific operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output; SDKs are platform dependent, with a platform being a combination of hardware and operating system (OS), and the developer may not handle the lowest-level operations directly but must understand the SDK that handles them.

defining_facts.text: In practical virtual reality (VR) development, a developer may use a software development kit (SDK) for a particular headset or platform to handle lowest-level, platform-specific operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output; SDKs are platform dependent, with a platform being a combination of hardware and operating system (OS), and the developer may not handle the lowest-level operations directly but must understand the SDK that handles them.

To build a virtual reality (VR) experience, a developer can either build a virtual world generator (VWG) from scratch using a basic software development kit (SDK) for a specific headset, device, or platform, or use a ready-made virtual world generator (VWG) customized by choosing menu options and writing high-level scripts.

A basic software development kit (SDK) for a headset, device, or platform is typically expected to provide basic drivers to drive the hardware, interfaces or application programming interfaces (APIs) to access tracking data, and application programming interfaces (APIs) to make calls to graphical rendering libraries; in a virtual world generator (VWG), basic drivers and tracking cover some aspects and rendering covers other aspects, but not every aspect of locomotion or matched motion, physics, or networked collaborative virtual reality (VR) experience is typically taken care of by the software development kit (SDK).

When building a virtual world generator (VWG) from a basic software development kit (SDK), the developer must build, at the very least, the physics support of the virtual world from scratch, handling problems such as movement of an avatar, collision detection, occurrence of collision and the response to it, lighting models, and audio support; sometimes collaborative virtual reality (VR) experience support is also required.

Using a basic software development kit (SDK) to build a virtual world generator (VWG) from scratch gives the developer maximum control and the ability to optimize performance because the developer can choose and implement the algorithms for physics support according to performance, rather than being forced to use whatever comes with a package.

Using a basic software development kit (SDK) to build a virtual world generator (VWG) from scratch imposes a difficult implementation burden and requires a lot of effort to understand and implement the overall system from scratch.

Deployment of a virtual reality (VR) application can be native application deployment, which requires software development kits (SDKs) tailored to the platform and hardware, or web application deployment, which allows the experience to be obtained remotely without a specific device.

A software development kit (SDK) is a collection of software development tools in one installable package specific to a hardware and operating system (OS) combination, providing fundamental tools to design, build, and test virtual reality (VR) experiences for specific platforms.

Native deployment software development kits (SDKs) can be categorized in two ways: by application type, as virtual reality (VR) or augmented reality (AR) applications, and by availability, as proprietary or open source.

Different head-mounted displays (HMDs) use different virtual reality (VR) software development kits (SDKs): the HTC Vive system can use the OpenVR SDK by Valve, the SteamVR SDK, or the VRTK SDK; the Oculus Rift uses the Oculus SDK; the Samsung Gear VR uses the Oculus Mobile SDK; the Sony PlayStation uses the PSVR SDK; and Google Daydream View or Google Cardboard uses the Google VR SDK.
The Google virtual reality (VR) software development kit (SDK) is open source but is no longer very much supported.

If a system is to be deployed on a specified hardware platform, head-mounted display (HMD), or smart glasses, and that platform provides features or functions not included in the built-in support provided by the Unity environment, the developer imports software development kits (SDKs) or packages to access and use those platform-specific functions.

In the Unity layered architecture, the application is the top layer, and the software development kit (SDK) layer, which is positioned on top of the Unity layer, is treated as part of the installed Unity package whose application programming interfaces (APIs) are used.

Vuforia is an augmented reality (AR) software development kit (SDK) primarily meant to help developers deal with object recognition or computer vision issues, such as object detection, recognition, and tracking.

The basic steps for integrating a software development kit (SDK) into the Unity development environment are to install Unity Hub, import the SDK package into the Unity environment, use the functions of both Unity and the SDK, and then compile, build, and deploy.

concepts.name: cybersickness
concepts.definition: Cybersickness (CS), also known in the literature as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR) technology and is primarily relevant to virtual reality.

defining_facts.text: Cybersickness (CS), also known in the literature as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR) technology and is primarily relevant to virtual reality.

A large number of symptoms may indicate the onset of cybersickness (CS) or cybersickness itself, and common ones include nausea, headache, excessive sweating, dryness of mouth, fullness of stomach, vomiting or a tendency to vomit, dizziness, disorientation, fatigue, and strange hand-eye coordination in which coordination does not happen in the expected way, so if one or more of these symptoms occur during a virtual reality (VR) experience, cybersickness can be assumed to be happening or going to happen.
Cybersickness (CS) can be caused by many factors, not by a single factor.

Reducing the impact of cybersickness (CS) is very important for usability and acceptability of virtual reality (VR) systems because it greatly enhances overall user experience and makes virtual reality applications more appealing to a wider range of people.

Another possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body may not be able to adapt, causing increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness, that is, dizziness, nausea, or a large set of different symptoms experienced while using virtual reality systems.

A sensory mismatch in a virtual reality (VR) system may be insignificant if the user's brain can adapt, but for other users it can cause cybersickness, with symptoms such as fatigue, headache, dizziness, and nausea.

Cybersickness, also known as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR), and it is not a single-factor effect because a variety of factors can affect it.

The factors that can induce cybersickness are broadly divided into internal factors, which include the age of the user, the gender of the user, the user's susceptibility to motion sickness, the physical condition of the user, and the emotional condition of the user, and external factors, which include hardware factors such as display resolution, latency, latency jitter, type of display, and type of input, and virtual reality (VR) content factors such as visual motion, means of locomotion, field of view, type of content, duration, and visual complexity.

Finding feasible solutions to reduce the impact of cybersickness while a user is experiencing virtual reality (VR) is important because it is supposed to greatly enhance overall user experience and make VR more appealing to a wider range of people.

Cybersickness mitigation strategies often come at the cost of presence because reducing cybersickness may make the user feel more in an artificial environment than in a real environment and less likely to obtain a proper immersive experience.

concepts.name: teleportation
concepts.definition: The type of transition, meaning how the scene changes from one field of view to another, is another aspect of locomotion that affects cybersickness (CS); teleportation, an instantaneous transition, is found to reduce cybersickness compared with naturalistic free movement such as walking, running, and jumping.

defining_facts.text: The type of transition, meaning how the scene changes from one field of view to another, is another aspect of locomotion that affects cybersickness (CS); teleportation, an instantaneous transition, is found to reduce cybersickness compared with naturalistic free movement such as walking, running, and jumping.

Teleportation in virtual reality (VR) is a locomotion operation in which a user can pull up a menu, point to a desired virtual location, and be sent to that location without making any physical movement.

Target selection-based locomotion techniques include teleportation, which instantly changes the virtual viewpoint from the current location to the target location, map dragging, in which the user fixes a location to move there instantly, and the jumper technique in cave-type systems.

Route planning-based locomotion is a selection-based locomotion technique in which the user selects a route to the target rather than only the endpoint; there may be multiple routes, and while moving through the selected route, different viewpoint changes make the user feel movement along a path, providing more granular control over travel and slightly more natural movement than target-based teleportation.

Teleportation-type movement in a virtual world can be the best choice for reducing overall exposure duration because it provides instantaneous movement between two points at maximum speed, but it is not a natural movement and may not always be a good approach when naturalness is required.

concepts.name: simulator sickness questionnaire
concepts.definition: The Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) is one of the most extensively used questionnaires for measuring cybersickness (CS).

defining_facts.text: The Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) is one of the most extensively used questionnaires for measuring cybersickness (CS).
The Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) contains 16 items divided into three subscales: the oculomotor subscale, the disorientation subscale, and the nausea subscale.

In the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ), participants rate the intensity of individual symptoms belonging to the oculomotor, disorientation, and nausea subscales on a scale from 0 to 3, where a higher score denotes more severe symptoms.
The Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) was not originally designed for virtual reality (VR) but was adapted for use in the context of virtual reality.
The simulator sickness questionnaire (SSQ) is the most extensively used of the questionnaires specifically designed for cyber sickness in extended reality (XR).

The simulator sickness questionnaire (SSQ) was used to measure cyber sickness, and it is a standard questionnaire that is popular for measuring cyber sickness in immersive experiences although it was not originally developed for cyber sickness.
Participants rated their cyber sickness symptoms on the simulator sickness questionnaire (SSQ) using a scale from 0 to 3, where 0 means no symptoms and 3 means the most severe symptoms.
The scores considered from the simulator sickness questionnaire (SSQ) were nausea, disorientation, oculomotor discomfort, and total sickness.

The participants' simulator sickness questionnaire (SSQ) scores were computed before and after exposure and compared to get an idea of the effect of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour assessment design on those scores.

concepts.definition: The International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 standard defines usability as the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

defining_facts.text: The International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 standard defines usability as the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

The three measures of usability are effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction; effectiveness is whether the user can do what they want to do, efficiency is how fast the user can do what they want to do, and satisfaction is how satisfied the user is when using the system.

concepts.name: navigation
concepts.definition: Interaction in immersive environments is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control, where object interaction means selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment, navigation means moving from one point to another in the virtual environment, and interaction for system control means interaction required to change system-related settings.

defining_facts.text: Interaction in immersive environments is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control, where object interaction means selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment, navigation means moving from one point to another in the virtual environment, and interaction for system control means interaction required to change system-related settings.

In the design of immersive experiences, interaction is broadly categorized into three categories: object interaction, which is interacting with virtual objects in the immersive virtual world; navigation, which is moving from one point in the virtual world to another point with the corresponding change in viewpoint and mostly does not involve object interaction, although some navigation techniques may require it; and system control, which is a mostly regular type of interaction used to set up the system, initialize parameters, provide initial information, and set options or menus, and is unlike object manipulation, object interaction, and navigation.
The goal of navigation in a virtual world is to move the user from one point to another, which means a change of the user's field of view or viewpoint.
The movement involved in navigation in a virtual world has two parts: the travel part and the wayfinding part.
Navigation has two components: locomotion or travel, which is the motor component, and wayfinding.

concepts.name: selection
concepts.definition: In any virtual experience, object interaction is broadly of two types: selection, which specifies one or more objects from a set of virtual objects in the virtual world, and manipulation, which interacts with a selected object to change its properties; the two types mostly have separate interaction techniques.

defining_facts.text: In any virtual experience, object interaction is broadly of two types: selection, which specifies one or more objects from a set of virtual objects in the virtual world, and manipulation, which interacts with a selected object to change its properties; the two types mostly have separate interaction techniques.

concepts.name: minimap
concepts.definition: A minimap is a world-in-miniature map for a specific place on the island, such as a village or town; it differs in appearance from the global island map and is provided at each of the island's 24 information points to give the user a sense of belonging or local orientation to that place.

defining_facts.text: A minimap is a world-in-miniature map for a specific place on the island, such as a village or town; it differs in appearance from the global island map and is provided at each of the island's 24 information points to give the user a sense of belonging or local orientation to that place.

On the minimap, white dots represent the arrangement of the 360-degree images; the user navigates by moving from one image to another along the dots, and the arrangement provides direction and orientation; the user's current image is highlighted green.

For location awareness, the system uses dual maps: a global map, which is a world-in-miniature map of the entire island, on the tablet interface and a local minimap on the local interface, to reduce clutter and provide clear navigation support.

The global map and the local minimap support wayfinding and orientation awareness by showing the entire world in miniature; the minimap provides dynamic spatial orientation awareness about which direction to move, helping users create a mental map and wayfind.

concepts.name: video player
concepts.definition: The virtual tablet interface provided to users acts as the main interface and provides navigation tools, a video player, and access to information content.

defining_facts.text: The virtual tablet interface provided to users acts as the main interface and provides navigation tools, a video player, and access to information content.
The video player in the virtual tablet interface has a volume controller and other controls and is used to view cultural videos or top-view drone videos of a place.

In the virtual tour system, the tablet interface includes a video player that allows users to access cultural and ecological videos relevant to the user's current location in the virtual world; the videos can be 360-degree videos, drone videos, or regular two-dimensional (2D) videos.

concepts.name: notification
concepts.definition: At each place, notifications alert users to available cultural videos; when there is something to see at a spot, the information icon becomes active, and selecting it shows whether a cultural video is available at that spot, which can be played on the tablet interface.

defining_facts.text: At each place, notifications alert users to available cultural videos; when there is something to see at a spot, the information icon becomes active, and selecting it shows whether a cultural video is available at that spot, which can be played on the tablet interface.

concepts.name: tablet interface
concepts.definition: In the virtual tour system, the tablet interface includes a video player that allows users to access cultural and ecological videos relevant to the user's current location in the virtual world; the videos can be 360-degree videos, drone videos, or regular two-dimensional (2D) videos.

defining_facts.text: In the virtual tour system, the tablet interface includes a video player that allows users to access cultural and ecological videos relevant to the user's current location in the virtual world; the videos can be 360-degree videos, drone videos, or regular two-dimensional (2D) videos.

The virtual tour system's tablet interface shows a list of videos available for a given spot, and when the user is at a spot the corresponding material for that spot is added to the interface so the user can choose it, giving access to the most relevant information for that spot, and that relevant information is also determined by the user type.

concepts.name: expert evaluation
concepts.definition: Quick evaluation of prototypes, also known as expert evaluation, is a technique for quickly and cheaply evaluating a prototype at an early stage of design, unlike a robust evaluation technique, which typically involves suitably skilled evaluators, resources, and an evaluation setup.

defining_facts.text: Quick evaluation of prototypes, also known as expert evaluation, is a technique for quickly and cheaply evaluating a prototype at an early stage of design, unlike a robust evaluation technique, which typically involves suitably skilled evaluators, resources, and an evaluation setup.
The prerequisites for performing quick or expert evaluation are at least a low-fidelity prototype, with higher-quality prototypes being better, and a team of evaluators.

Quick evaluation is a usability test, but although the primary condition of usability testing is to involve users, the evaluation team for quick or expert evaluation is primarily the design team itself or skilled designers with knowledge and skill in the problem domain, and may optionally include a few end users.

Quick or expert evaluation can rely on design-team members or domain experts rather than end users because they are assumed to have user-like experience, their feedback likely reflects users, and engaging them is less complicated, quicker, and cheaper than engaging a full evaluation team with end users.
The evaluation team for expert evaluation should have at least three to five members; more members are welcome, but three to five is sufficient.

In expert evaluation, each evaluator is presented with the prototype, evaluates it independently, and produces a report containing the usability issues perceived by that evaluator; the design team or team lead then combines these reports into a final list of usability issues.

never_defined.name: headset
never_defined.definition: To different people, hearing extended reality (XR), virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), or mixed reality (MR) may lead them to associate one or more of these terms with magical movie scenes such as those in Avatar, interactive video games, 3D or 4D movie-theater documentaries about extinct animals, a user wearing a headset that blocks vision and transports the user to a virtual world, which is the most common perception of VR, games such as Pokémon Go in which the real world is visible on a device screen and virtual objects that do not exist in the real world can also be seen on that screen, or visualizations of internal body structures such as a skeleton or veins.

never_defined.name: two-dimensional image
never_defined.definition: Sir Charles Wheatstone's 1838 demonstration of a stereoscopic device established, for the first time in recorded history, that the human brain can process two-dimensional (2D) images as three-dimensional (3D) objects, and this demonstration is roughly considered a first step toward immersive experience.

never_defined.name: smartphone
never_defined.definition: In 2004, the first mobile-phone based augmented reality (AR) application was demonstrated and the AR Toolkit was ported to mobile phones, and although early mobile phones looked different from modern-day smartphones, people still tried to use early mobile phones to develop mobile-based augmented reality applications.

never_defined.name: 360-degree video
never_defined.definition: The highest representational fidelity is indicated by very good photorealistic immersive film content, such as 360-degree video or images of the real world in a virtual environment, while extremely low representational fidelity is indicated by purely abstract and non-objective worlds that are unfamiliar in real-world experience.

never_defined.name: cyber sickness susceptibility
never_defined.definition: Age is related to cyber sickness susceptibility: children aged 2 to 12 may show increased sensitivity, that tendency decreases as they grow older, older persons are likely to experience higher levels, cyber sickness is generally uncommon among young children, and it is highly unlikely in users aged 12 to 25.

never_defined.name: Virtual Reality Sickness Questionnaire
never_defined.definition: Questionnaires specifically designed for virtual reality (VR) include the Virtual Reality Sickness Questionnaire (VRSQ) and the Cyber Sickness Questionnaire (CSQ), which is good for evaluating virtual reality experiences with head-mounted displays (HMDs).

never_defined.name: Misery Scale
never_defined.definition: Shorter and more concise questionnaires used to assess specific conditions include the Misery Scale (MIS) and the Fast Motion Sickness Scale (FMS).

never_defined.definition: Shorter and more concise questionnaires used to assess specific conditions include the Misery Scale (MIS) and the Fast Motion Sickness Scale (FMS).

never_defined.definition: The outputs of self-report questionnaires for cybersickness (CS) are generally scores or ratings on rating scales, and these scores or ratings can be used to assess the severity of cybersickness.

never_defined.name: map
never_defined.definition: Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) is a technique that simultaneously creates and updates a map of the real environment while localizing positions within it, and as time passes the map is updated with the object's changing position, enabling real-time tracking.

never_defined.name: three-dimensional model
never_defined.definition: 3D structure tracking (3D structure sensing) is a recent tracking technique that uses commercial sensors to obtain the 3D positions of points in the scene and creates 3D models of the structures in the environment for augmentation of the real-world view.

never_defined.name: operating system

never_defined.name: Android

never_defined.name: interactive system

never_defined.name: object

never_defined.name: expert evaluation technique
never_defined.definition: Unlike expert evaluation techniques, which give designers more detailed reports from each evaluator, the System Usability Scale (SUS) gives a quick general indication from user ratings of whether usability problems exist but does not explain the reasons, so designers must identify the specific problems through further brainstorming or by examining the scores of individual statements.
